1.pericope_label: Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted

schools.summary: Work the verb first. The word rendered be overtaken means properly to take before another, to anticipate, and then to be before taken or caught; it may mean either that one had been formerly guilty of sin or that he had been recently hurried on by passion or temptation, and the latter is probably the sense — if a man is found to be overtaken by any sin, if his passions or a temptation get the better of him. Tindal renders it, if any man be fallen by chance into any fault. It refers to cases of surprise or of sudden temptation. Christians do not commit sin deliberately, as a part of the plan of life, but they may be surprised by sudden temptation or urged on by headlong passion, as David and Peter were. Draw the limit sharply: Paul does not speak of the possibility of restoring one who deliberately forms the plan of sinning; he does not suppose that such a man could be a Christian, nor that it would be proper to speak of restoring him. Ye which are spiritual means those under the influences of the Holy Spirit. Elsewhere press the detection harder: the word means not only caught, but caught red-handed, in the very act, before he can escape — a special expression used in order to aggravate the circumstances of the detection; and no matter what these circumstances may be, one who is truly spiritual will still deal gently with the offender. Note that the appeal opens with Brethren, whose conventional use rather tends to weaken our sense of the delicacy and earnestness of the appeal. Restore is a good translation: the idea is that of correcting with no feeling of resentment or thought of punishment, but with a single eye to the amendment of the offender, the same word being used for mending their nets in the Gospels and found also as a medical term for setting dislocated limbs. On the spirit of meekness, say that spirit here has reference to ye that are spiritual in the clause before: it does not mean exactly the Holy Spirit, but such a state of mind as is produced by the operation of the Spirit, and one characteristic of a truly spiritual state is meekness, which is named expressly among the fruits of the Spirit. Considering thyself means, in other words, do unto others as ye would they should do unto you: you too are liable to fall, and then you would be glad of the same gentle restoration. Elsewhere again, keep to the grammar and the papyri. The condition is of the third class, with the first aorist passive subjunctive of an old verb meaning to take beforehand, to surprise, to detect. The word for trespass is literally a falling aside, and in the papyri a slip or lapse rather than a wilful sin. The spiritual are the spiritually led, the spiritual experts in mending souls. Restore is the present active imperative of the verb used of mending nets, an old word meaning to make fit, to equip thoroughly. Looking to thyself is keeping an eye on oneself, like a runner on the goal. And add the warning about who needs the warning: spiritual experts, preachers in particular, need this caution, for Satan loves a shining mark.

Settle what kind of fault is meant, and against whom the verse is not aimed. Overtaken means taken before — not, as Grotius thinks, before this epistle should come to them, which is a very jejune and empty sense of the words; nor before the man’s conversion, because sins before conversion do not come under the cognizance of a church or are liable to its censures; but before the man is aware, through negligence and imprudence, for want of caution and circumspection, so that he is carried away, either through the treachery of his own heart and the power of corruption, or through the temptations of Satan, who goes about and comes on the back of them, lays snares for them and attacks them unawares, or by the ill examples of others. The apostle has no particular respect by a fault to schisms in the church, or to errors or heresies in doctrine, though the restoration of such should be endeavoured in meekness, but rather to immorality in life and conversation, and indeed to any of the works of the flesh mentioned in the preceding chapter. Then take the manner of the correction, and be severe about the severe. Ambition is a serious and alarming evil, but hardly less injury is frequently done by unseasonable and excessive severity, which, under the plausible name of zeal, springs in many instances from pride, and from dislike and contempt of the brethren. Most men seize on the faults of brethren as an occasion of insulting them, and of using reproachful and cruel language; were the pleasure they take in upbraiding equalled by their desire to produce amendment, they would act in a different manner. Reproof, and often sharp and severe reproof, must be administered to offenders; but while we must not shrink from a faithful testimony against sin, neither must we omit to mix oil with the vinegar. Explain the design of pious reproofs, which is to place the offender in his former condition — a design that will never be accomplished by violence, or by a disposition to accuse, or by fierceness of manner or language. And lest any man satisfy himself with assuming the outward form, insist on the spirit: no man is prepared for chastising a brother till he has succeeded in acquiring a gentle spirit, and we are to consider no rebukes as partaking a religious and Christian character which do not breathe the spirit of meekness. Take the word overtaken as a second argument for gentleness: if he has been carried away through want of consideration, or through the cunning arts of a deceiver, it would be cruel to treat such a man with harshness. The devil is always lying in wait, and has a thousand ways of leading us astray; when we perceive a brother to have transgressed, let us consider that he has fallen into the snares of Satan, be moved with compassion, and prepare our minds to exercise forgiveness. But distinguish these offences from deep-seated crimes accompanied by deliberate and obstinate disregard of the authority of God: such a display of wicked and perverse disobedience must be visited with greater severity, for what advantage would be gained by gentle treatment? Note finally that ye which are spiritual is not spoken in irony — however spiritual they might be, they were not wholly filled with the Spirit — and that the more eminently any man is endowed with divine grace, the more strongly is he bound to consult the edification of those less favoured.

Put the verse in its place first: having exhorted Christians by love to serve one another, and cautioned them against a temper which would hinder that love, the apostle now gives further directions which would both promote the one and prevent the other. He puts a common case: if a man be overtaken in a fault, that is, be brought to sin by the surprise of temptation. It is one thing to overtake a fault by contrivance and deliberation and a full resolution in sin, and another thing to be overtaken in a fault; the latter is the case supposed, and herein great tenderness should be used. By those who are spiritual is meant not only the ministers — as if none but they were to be called spiritual persons — but other Christians too, especially those of the higher form in Christianity. Then set out three things. The duty: we should labour, by faithful reproofs and by pertinent and seasonable counsels, to bring them to repentance; the original word signifies to set in joint, as a dislocated bone, and accordingly we should endeavour to set them in joint again, to bring them to themselves by convincing them of their sin and error, persuading them to return to their duty, comforting them in a sense of pardoning mercy thereupon, and, having thus recovered them, confirming our love to them. The manner: with the spirit of meekness, not in wrath and passion, as those who triumph in a brother’s falls, but with meekness, as those who rather mourn for them — for many needful reproofs lose their efficacy by being given in wrath, whereas when they are managed with calmness and tenderness, and appear to proceed from sincere affection and concern for the welfare of those to whom they are given, they are likely to make a due impression. And the reason: considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted. We ought to deal very tenderly with those who are overtaken in sin, because none of us knows but it may some time or other be our own case; we also may be tempted, yea, and overcome by the temptation, and therefore, if we rightly consider ourselves, this will dispose us to do by others as we would desire to be done by in such a case.

Begin with the word and let a classical illustration carry it. Overtaken means surprised, seized on without warning, suddenly invaded, taken before he is aware: Strabo applies the same verb to the rhinoceros in its contests with the elephant, which endeavours to rip up the elephant’s belly with the horn on its nose so that he may not first be surprised by the trunk, since should the elephant seize him with the trunk first, all resistance would afterwards be in vain; and Arrian uses it of a vessel suddenly agitated and whirled by the waves and then dashed on the rocks. Ye which are spiritual means ye who still retain the grace of the Gospel and have wisdom and experience in divine things — who continue to live and walk by the Spirit. Restore such a one means bring the man back into his place: it is a metaphor taken from a dislocated limb brought back by the hand of a skilful and tender surgeon into its place; and the restoring is done by reproof, instruction or exhortation, in which every one who can ought to help. In the spirit of meekness means use no severity nor haughty carriage towards him: as the man was suddenly overtaken, he is already deeply humbled and distressed, and needs much encouragement and lenient usage. Insist that this is essential to a spiritual man, and that in it lies the whole force of the cure. Mark the great difference between a man who, being suddenly assailed, falls into sin, and the man who transgressed in consequence of having walked in the counsel of the ungodly or stood in the way of sinners. Considering thyself means looking to thyself: as he fell through a moment of unwatchfulness, look about that thou be not surprised; as he fell, so mayest thou; thou art now warned at his expense, therefore keep a good look out. And note the grammatical turn, that the plural is beautifully changed into the singular — let each take heed to himself. Lest thou also be tempted: having had this warning, thou wilt have the less to plead in extenuation of thy offence; temptation easily and swiftly passes from one to another, especially if a man endeavours to cure another without preserving his own meekness. It is no wonder if a harsh and cruel censurer of a weak, backsliding brother should be taught moderation and mercy by an awful proof of his own frailty. From the consideration of what we are, what we have been, or what we may be, we should learn to be compassionate.

Weigh the apostle’s words closely and see what he does not say. He that diligently weigheth them may plainly perceive that he speaketh not of errors and offences against doctrine, but of far lesser sins, into which a man falleth not wilfully and of set purpose, but of infirmity. Hereof it cometh that he useth so gentle and fatherly a word, not calling it error or sin, but a fault. Again, to the intent to diminish, and as it were to excuse the sin, and to remove the whole fault from man, he addeth, if any man be overtaken — that is to say, be beguiled of the devil or of the flesh. Yea, and this term or name of man helpeth something also to diminish and qualify the matter: as if he should say, what is so proper unto man as to fall, to be deceived, and to err? So saith Moses, they are wont to sin like men. Wherefore this is a sentence full of heavenly comfort, which once in a terrible conflict delivered me from death. Forasmuch then as the saints in this life do not only live in the flesh, but now and then also, through the enticement of the devil, fulfil the lust of the flesh — that is to say, fall into impatiency, envy, wrath, error, doubting, distrust and such like, for Satan always assaileth both the purity of doctrine, which he laboureth to take away by sects and dissensions, and the soundness of life, which he corrupteth with daily offences — therefore Paul teacheth how such men that are fallen should be dealt withal, namely, that they which are strong should raise them up and restore them again with the spirit of meekness. These things it behoveth them specially to know which are in the ministry of the word, lest, whilst they go about to touch all things to the quick, they forget the fatherly and motherly affection which Paul here requireth of those that have the charge of souls. He hath set forth an example of this precept where he saith that it was sufficient that he which was excommunicate was rebuked of many, and that they ought now to forgive him and comfort him, lest he should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. Wherefore, saith he, I beseech you, use charity towards him. Therefore the pastors and ministers must indeed sharply rebuke those which are fallen; but when they see that they are sorrowful for their offences, then let them begin to raise them up again, to comfort them, and to diminish and qualify their faults as much as they can, but yet through mercy only, which they must set against sin, lest they that be fallen be swallowed up with overmuch heaviness. As the Holy Ghost is precise in maintaining and defending the doctrine of faith, so is he mild and pitiful in forbearing and qualifying men’s sins, if they which have committed them be sorrowful for the same. But the Pope’s synagogue hath both taught and done clean contrary to the commandment and example of Paul in this thing as in all others: the Pope with all his bishops have been very tyrants and butchers of men’s consciences, burdening them from time to time with new traditions, and for every light matter vexing them with their excommunications.

Fix on the three words the apostle chose. He says not chastise, nor judge, but set right. Nor does he stop there; but in order to show that it behoved them to be very gentle towards those who had lost their footing, he subjoins, in a spirit of meekness. He says not in meekness, but in a spirit of meekness, signifying thereby that this is acceptable to the Spirit, and that to be able to administer correction with mildness is a spiritual gift. Then, to prevent the one being unduly exalted by having to correct the other, he puts him under the same fear.

debates: Whether overtaken means surprised by temptation or caught in the act.
What kind of fault is in view — doctrinal error or immorality of life.
Whether the spirit of meekness means the Holy Spirit or a state of mind.
Who the spiritual are, and whether ministers only.
How gentleness toward the fallen is bounded.
outliers: Clarke illustrates the verb from Strabo on the rhinoceros and the elephant.
Luther reports that this verse once delivered him from death in a terrible conflict.
Gill rejects Grotius’s reading of overtaken as a very jejune and empty sense of the words.
Calvin insists that ye which are spiritual is not spoken in irony.
Barnes uses the verse to deny that a deliberate planner of sin could be a Christian at all.

2.pericope_label: Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ. For if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself

schools.summary: Say what the burden is: every man has peculiar temptations and easily besetting sins, which constitute a heavy burden, and we should aid each other in regard to these and help one another to overcome them. The law of Christ is the peculiar law of the Redeemer, requiring us to love one another, and they could in no way better fulfil it than by aiding each other in the divine life. Press the pastoral consequence hard. The law of Christ would not allow us to reproach the offender, or to taunt him, or to rejoice in his fall; we should help him to take up his load of infirmities and sustain him by our counsels, our exhortations and our prayers. Christians, conscious of their infirmities, have a right to the sympathy and the prayers of their brethren; they should not be cast off to a cold and heartless world, a world rejoicing over their fall and ready to brand them as hypocrites, but should be pressed to the warm bosom of brotherly kindness, and prayer should be made without ceasing around an erring and fallen brother. Then ask the question and leave it standing: is this the case in regard to all who bear the Christian name? On the third verse, take it as another reason to be kind and tender to those who have erred, namely that even the most confident may fall: they who feel secure, and think it impossible that they should sin, are not safe. When he is nothing means when he has no strength and no moral worth, when he is not such as he apprehends but is lifted up with vain self-conceit; and he deceiveth himself means that he understands not his own character — the worst part of the fraud falls on his own head — so that instead of acquiring reputation from others, as he expected, he renders himself contemptible in their sight. Elsewhere take the burden bearing as a courtesy of sympathy: take them upon yourselves by kindly sympathy, as our Lord himself was said to bear the physical infirmities of those whom he healed. Weigh the reading of the verb: for the received text, so fulfil, is a large majority of the manuscripts, but the reading ye shall fulfil is found in the Vatican and two good Graeco-Latin manuscripts and has besides an almost unanimous support from the versions, several composed at a very early date and necessarily representing a wide geographical dispersion; the manuscript authority, though small in quantity, is good in quality and also represents widely separated regions; and the internal probabilities of corruption are in favour of the same reading, so that on the whole it seems to have the greater claim to acceptance. The meaning is that by showing sympathy to others in their distress, of whatever kind that distress may be, whether physical, mental or moral, the Christian will best fulfil the new commandment bequeathed to him by his Master, the law of love. On he deceiveth himself, note a peculiar word, perhaps coined by St Paul: he puts himself under an hallucination, and persuades himself of the existence of that which has no reality. Elsewhere again, keep to the grammar. Bear is the present active imperative, keep on bearing, of the verb used of Jesus bearing his cross; the noun means weight, and the point is the moment when one’s load is about to press one down — then give help in carrying it. Fulfil is the first aorist active imperative of the verb to fill up, though some manuscripts have the future indicative. On the third verse: he thinks he is a big number, being nothing at all — he is really zero. The verb rendered he deceiveth himself is a late compound from mind and to lead astray, found here for the first time and afterwards in Galen and the ecclesiastical and Byzantine writers: he leads his own mind astray, and he deceives no one else.

Distinguish the senses of burden before applying the command. The burdens may be sins, which are heavy burdens to sensible sinners, to all that are partakers of the grace of God; but Christ only is able to bear these so as to remove them and take them away, which he has done by his blood, sacrifice and satisfaction. Saints bear one another’s not by making satisfaction for them, which they are not able to do, nor by conniving at them and suffering them upon them, which they should not do, but by gently reproving them, by comforting them when overpressed with guilt, by sympathising with them in their sorrow, by praying to God to manifest his pardoning grace to them, and by forgiving them themselves so far as they are faults committed against them. Or the burdens may be the frailties and infirmities of weak saints, which are troublesome and apt to make uneasy; and these are to be borne by the strong, by making themselves easy with them, by accommodating themselves to their weakness, and by abridging themselves of some liberties which otherwise might lawfully be taken. Or afflictions may be designed, which are grievous to the flesh. Then ground the duty and guard it. The weaknesses or sins under which we groan are called burdens, and the phrase is singularly appropriate in an exhortation to kind behaviour, for nature dictates to us that those who bend under a burden ought to be relieved. But we must not indulge or overlook the sins by which our brethren are pressed down; we are to relieve them, which can only be done by mild and friendly correction. There are many adulterers and thieves, many wicked and abandoned characters of every description, who would willingly make Christ an accomplice in their crimes, and all would choose to lay upon believers the task of bearing their burdens; but since the apostle has immediately before exhorted us to restore a brother, the manner in which Christians are required to bear cannot be mistaken. On the law of Christ, note that the word law, applied here to Christ, serves the place of an argument, and that there is an implied contrast between the law of Christ and the law of Moses: if you are very desirous to keep a law, Christ enjoins on you a law which you are bound to prefer to all others, and that is to cherish kindness towards each other; he who has not this has nothing. Everything which does not proceed from love is superfluous; and the composition of the Greek word conveys the idea of what is absolutely perfect, so that, as no man performs in every respect what Paul requires, we are still at a distance from perfection — he who comes the nearest to it with regard to others is yet far distant with respect to God. On the third verse, resolve the construction. The phrase appears at first view to mean, if any person who is in reality nothing claims to be something, as there are many men of no real worth who are elated by a foolish admiration of themselves; but the meaning is more general: since all men are nothing, he who wishes to appear something, and persuades himself that he is somebody, deceives himself. First he declares that we are nothing, meaning that we have nothing of our own of which we have a right to boast, but are destitute of everything good, so that all our glorying is mere vanity; secondly he infers that they who claim something as their own deceive themselves. Now since nothing excites our indignation more than that others should impose upon us, it argues the height of folly that we should willingly impose upon ourselves; and this consideration will render us much more candid to others. Whence proceeds fierce insult or haughty sternness, but from this, that every one exalts himself in his own estimation and proudly despises others? Let arrogance be removed, and we shall all discover the greatest modesty in our conduct towards each other. Note also that thinking oneself something means of oneself — to have anything of oneself, to do anything of oneself, and of oneself to attain to life and salvation.

Make the command sympathy before it is action. Bear ye one another’s burdens means have sympathy, feel for each other, and consider the case of a distressed brother as your own; sympathise with, and assist, each other in all your weaknesses, grievances and trials. And so fulfil the law of Christ means that law or commandment, ye shall love one another, or that other, do unto all men as ye would they should do unto you. The law of Christ is an uncommon expression, and it is the law of love: this our Lord peculiarly recommends, and this he makes the distinguishing mark of his disciples. We should be as indulgent to the infirmities of others as we can be consistently with truth and righteousness; our brother’s infirmity may be his burden, and if we do not choose to help him to bear it, let us not reproach him because he is obliged to carry the load. On the third verse, say what the something is: to think himself to be something is to think himself a proper Christian man, or to think himself above his brethren, or possessed of some strength of his own, when he is nothing, being destitute of that charity which beareth, hopeth and endureth all things. Then name the type. Those who suppose themselves to excel all others in piety and understanding, while they are harsh, censorious and overbearing, prove that they have not the charity that thinketh no evil, and in the sight of God are only as sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal. There are no people more censorious or uncharitable than those among some religious people who pretend to more light and a deeper communion with God; they are generally carried away with a sort of sublime, high-sounding phraseology which seems to argue a wonderfully deep acquaintance with divine things, and stripped of this many of them are like Samson without his hair. Close with the rule that follows from it: he alone will bear their burdens who knows himself to be nothing.

Commend the gentleness of the commandment, then turn it against the sectaries. This is a gentle commandment, to which is joined a great commendation; for the law of Christ is the law of love, and Christ, after he had redeemed us, renewed us and made us his church, gave us no other law but the law of mutual love: a new commandment give I unto you, that ye love one another. On the third verse, here again he reprehendeth the authors of sects and painteth them out in their right colours — to wit, that they be hard-hearted, merciless and without compassion, such as despise the weak and will not vouchsafe to bear their burdens, but require all things straitly and precisely, like wayward husbands and severe schoolmasters, whom nothing can please but what they themselves do, and who will be always thy bitter enemies unless thou commend whatsoever they say or do and in all things frame thyself according to their appetite. Of all men therefore they are the proudest, and dare take upon them all things. And this is that Paul saith here: they think themselves to be somewhat, that is to say, that they have the Holy Ghost, that they understand all the mysteries of the Scriptures, that they cannot err. Wherefore Paul addeth very well that they are nothing, but that they deceive themselves with the foolish persuasions of their own wisdom and holiness. They understand nothing therefore either of Christ or of the law of Christ; for if they did, they would say, Brother, thou art infected with such a vice, and I am infected with another; God hath forgiven me ten thousand talents, and I will forgive thee an hundred pence. But when they will require all things so exactly and with such perfection, and will in no wise bear the burdens of the weak, they offend many with this their sharpness and severity, who begin to despise, hate and shun them, and seek not comfort or counsel at their hands, nor regard what or how they teach. Whereas contrariwise, pastors ought so to behave themselves towards those over whom they have taken charge that they might love and reverence them, not for their person, but for their office and the Christian virtues which especially ought to shine in them. For it is a manifest beguiling when a man persuadeth himself that he is somewhat, when indeed he is nothing.

debates: What the burdens are — sins, infirmities, or afflictions.
Whether the text reads so fulfil or ye shall fulfil.
What the law of Christ is, and how it stands to the law of Moses.
Whether the nothing of verse 3 is said of a class of men or of all men.
outliers: Ellicott prefers the minority reading ye shall fulfil on the strength of the early versions.
Calvin generalises the nothing to all men, so that the self-deceived man is any man who claims anything as his own.
Gill insists Christ alone can bear sins so as to remove them, and lists what bearing can and cannot mean for saints.
Luther identifies the man who thinks himself something with the authors of sects.
Barnes turns the verse into a question about the churches of his own day.

4.pericope_label: But let every man prove his own work, and then shall he have rejoicing in himself alone, and not in another. For every man shall bear his own burden

schools.summary: Define the proving. Let every man try or examine in a proper manner, forming a proper estimate of what is due to himself according to his real character; let him compare himself with the word of God, the infallible rule which he has given and by which we are to be judged in the last great day. His own work means what he does; let him form a fair and impartial estimate of his own character. Then shall he have rejoicing means that he will be appropriately rewarded and will meet with no disappointment: the man who forms an improper estimate of his own character will be sure to be disappointed, while the man who examines himself, and forms no extravagant expectation of what is due to him, will be rewarded and made happy. If by careful examination he finds his life virtuous and his conduct pure, if he has done no wrong to others, and if he finds evidence that he is a child of God, then he has cause of rejoicing. In himself alone: a good man shall be satisfied from himself; he will find in himself a source of pure joy and will not be dependent on the applause of others for happiness. In an approving conscience, in the evidence of the favour of God, in an honest effort to lead a pure and holy life, he will have happiness; the source of his joys will be within, and he will not be dependent — as the man of ambition is, and the man who thinks of himself more highly than he ought — on the favours of a capricious multitude and the breath of popular applause. On the fifth verse, treat it as a kind of proverbial saying meaning that every man shall have his proper reward: if he is a virtuous man he will be happy, if a vicious man he will be miserable; in the great day every man shall be properly rewarded. Knowing this, we should be little anxious about the sentiments of others, and should seek to maintain a good conscience towards God and man. The design of the passage is to prevent men from forming an improper estimate of themselves and of the opinions of others: let a man feel that he is soon to stand at the judgment seat, and that his great interests are to be determined by the estimate which God will affix to his character, and it will teach him that the opinion of the world is of little value; there is no way so effectual of checking ambition, and subduing vanity and the love of applause, as to feel that we are soon to stand at the awful bar of God. Elsewhere fix the words. Prove means test, or examine, by reference to an objective standard, the word being used specially of the assaying of metals. Rejoicing in himself alone and not in another means rather that he shall have his ground of boasting with reference to himself alone, and not with reference to his neighbour: he will judge his own actions by the standard properly applicable to them, and will find as much ground for boasting as this will give him, and no more; his standard will be absolute and not relative, and the amount of his boasting proportioned accordingly, so that he will not seek to excuse himself by dwelling upon his neighbour’s weaknesses. On the fifth verse, note that the word for burden is different from the one used above, though its meaning is very much the same — the distinction would be sufficiently represented by translating burden in the one case and load in the other — but the context is quite different: there the Christian is bidden to bear the burdens of others in the sense of sympathising with them in their troubles, here he is told that he must bear his own load in the sense that he must answer directly to God for his own actions. His responsibility cannot be shifted on to others, and it will make him no better that there are others worse than himself. Add the lexical caution: the word is an old one for a ship’s cargo, and Christ calls his own load light though he terms those of the Pharisees heavy and meant for other people, so the terms are not always kept distinct, though Paul does make a distinction here.

Turn the man’s attention homeward. Let every man prove his own work: not concern himself about the actions and works of others, but review his own heart and actions, and examine, try and prove his whole conduct in life by the rule of God’s word — when he will find enough at home, without bearing hard upon and censuring others. Then explain why the rule is necessary. By a powerful blow Paul has already struck down the pride of man; but it frequently happens that, by comparing ourselves with others, the low opinion which we form of them leads us to entertain a high opinion of ourselves, and Paul declares that no such comparison ought to be allowed. Let no man measure himself by the standard of another, or please himself with the thought that others appear to him less worthy of approbation; let him lay aside all regard to other men, examine his own conscience, and inquire what is his own. It is not what we gain by detracting from others, but what we have without any comparison, that can be regarded as true praise. Report the ironical interpretation and reject it. Some consider Paul to be speaking in irony — thou flatterest thyself by a comparison with the faults of others, but if thou wilt consider who thou art, thou wilt then enjoy the praise which is justly due to thee, which is to say that no praise whatever shall be thine, because there is no man by whom the smallest portion of praise is really deserved; and in conformity with that view the following words are supposed to mean that it is usual for every man to bear his own burden. But the plain and direct sense of the words agrees better with the apostle’s reasoning: with respect to thyself alone, and not by comparison with others, thou wilt have praise. The next sentence, which annihilates all the glory of man, has been regarded as justifying the ironical interpretation; but the glorying of which this passage treats is that of a good conscience, in which the Lord allows his people to indulge, and which Paul elsewhere expresses in very animated language when, earnestly beholding the council, he said, Men and brethren, I have lived in all good conscience before God until this day. This is nothing more than an acknowledgment of divine grace, which reflects no praise whatever on man. On the fifth verse: to destroy sloth and pride he brings before us the judgment of God, in which every individual for himself, and without a comparison with others, will give an account of his life. It is thus that we are deceived; for if a man who has but one eye is placed among the blind, he considers his vision to be perfect, and a tawny person among negroes thinks himself white. The apostle affirms that the false conclusions to which we are thus conducted will find no place in the judgment of God, because there every one will bear his own burden, and none will stand acquitted by others from their own sins. Say also what the burden may be: either the work which God has allotted a man to do, whether in a more public or private station, which, because it is generally troublesome to the flesh, is called a burden, and his own, being peculiar to himself; or the account of his own actions, and not another’s, which he shall give to God in the other world, being judged according to his own works, what they are in themselves, and not by a comparison of other men’s who have been more wicked than he, which will be no rule of judgment with God nor of any advantage to man; or the punishment of his own sins, since the judgments of God inflicted on men in this world are often called a burden.

Make Christ the touchstone. Let him examine himself and his conduct by the words and example of Christ; and if he finds that they bear this touchstone, then he shall have rejoicing in himself alone, feeling that he resembles his Lord and Master — and not in another, that is, he will not derive his consolation from comparing himself with another who may be weaker or less instructed than himself. The only rule for a Christian is the word of Christ; the only pattern for his imitation is the example of Christ. He should not compare himself with others; they are not his standard. Christ hath left us an example that we should follow his steps. Put the examination plainly: narrowly examine all he is, and all he doeth; then he will find in himself matter of rejoicing, if his works are right before God, and not in glorying over others. On the fifth verse, draw the consequence: all must answer for themselves, not for their neighbours, and every man must expect to be dealt with by the divine Judge as his character and conduct have been. The greater offences of another will not excuse thy smaller crimes. Every man must give account of himself to God.

Take the fifth verse as the reason and confirmation of what goes before, lest any man lean to other men’s judgments in praising and commending him. As if he said, it is extreme madness for thee to seek glory in another, and not in thyself; for in the agony of death, and in the last judgment, it shall nothing profit thee that other men have praised thee, for other men shall not bear thy burden, but thou shalt stand before the judgment seat of Christ and shalt bear thy burden alone. There thy praisers shall nothing help thee, for when we die these praises shall cease. And in that day, when the Lord shall judge the secrets of all hearts, the witness of thine own conscience shall stand either with thee or against thee — against thee, if thou glory in other men; with thee, if thou have it in thyself, that is to say, if thy conscience bear thee witness that thou hast done thy duty in the ministry of the word, or otherwise according to thy calling, sincerely and faithfully, having respect to the glory of God only and the salvation of souls. These words are very vehement, and ought so to terrify us that we should not be desirous of vainglory. And this moreover is to be noted, that we are not here in the matter of justification, where nothing availeth but mere grace and forgiveness of sins, which is received by faith alone, and where all our works, yea even our best works, and such as are done according to God’s calling, have need of forgiveness of sins. But this is another case: he treateth not here of the remission of sins, but compareth true works and hypocritical works together.

debates: Whether the promise of rejoicing in oneself is spoken in irony.
What standard a man is to prove his work by.
Whether verse 5 contradicts verse 2, and what the two words for burden mean.
What burden a man bears at the judgment.
outliers: Calvin reports and rejects the ironical reading of the promise of rejoicing.
Ellicott separates the two words as burden and load, and makes the difference one of context rather than sense.
Robertson notes that Christ calls his own load light, so the two words are not always kept distinct.
Luther interrupts to insist that the passage is not about justification at all.

6.pericope_label: Let him that is taught in the word communicate unto him that teacheth in all good things. Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap

schools.summary: Take the first verse as a plain duty and the second as a principle. Him that is taught in the word means in the word of God, that is, the gospel; communicate unto him means let him share with him who teaches, let there be a common participation of all good things — in everything that is needful for their comfortable subsistence — and refer for the duty to what is said at length elsewhere about those who preach the gospel living of the gospel. On the warning, say that be not deceived is a formula of introduction to an admonition peculiarly weighty and important, and that it implies real danger of self-deception as to character, the sources of the danger being the corruption of their own hearts, the difficulty of knowing their true character, and the instructions of false teachers. God is not mocked means he cannot be imposed on: he knows what our real character is, and will judge us accordingly. The word rendered mocked means properly to turn up the nose in scorn, and hence to mock, deride or insult; here it cannot mean to imitate or mimic, but refers to the principles of the divine administration, which could not be treated with contempt or successfully evaded — they could not hope to illude or impose on God, whose principles of government were settled. In the connexion in which it stands it refers to the support of the ministers of the gospel, and the apostle introduces the general principle, that as a man sows he will reap, to show what will be the effect of a liberal and proper use of their property. Elsewhere note what the verse discloses about the church. He who receives instruction in the truths of the gospel is meant; and even at this early date there seems to have been a more or less organised system of instruction in the Church, teaching being regarded as a separate function, though those who took part in it do not seem as yet to have formed a separate class. The teacher was dependent on the alms of his scholars: he would receive no settled and regular payment, but the scholar would make him presents, many of them probably in kind, so as to relieve him from the care of providing for his own livelihood and give him more leisure for his work of teaching. On the warning, paraphrase it: it is all very well for you to make large professions to which you do not act up; these may deceive others, but do not let them deceive yourselves, and do not think that God will allow you thus to mock him. Concede that the language of the warning might seem almost too solemn for the occasion, an exhortation to liberality towards teachers, but say that the apostle has in mind the wider scope he is about to give the subject: with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again. Compare the parallel where the same metaphor is used of the same thing, that he which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly, and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully. Elsewhere again keep to the words. The verb for being taught is late and rare, occurring in the papyri for legal instruction, and the present passive participle retains the accusative of the thing; the active joined with the passive is interesting as showing how early we find paid teachers in the churches, and contribute is better than communicate for the verb used. There was a teaching class thus early. Be not deceived is a present passive imperative: stop being led astray. The verb rendered mocked is rare, comes from the word for nose, and means to turn the nose up at one; that is done towards God, but never without punishment — the thing meant is an evasion of his laws which men think to accomplish but in fact cannot. Whatsoever a man soweth is an indefinite relative clause, and one of the most frequent of ancient proverbs; that means that very thing, not something different.

Say who the taught man is, and then why the teachers are neglected. He that is taught in the word is, according to the original, a catechumen; and this designs not one just beginning to learn the first principles of the oracles of God, but anyone instructed in it, whether more or less, and whether internally or externally. One internally taught by the word has been taught to know himself and his lost state by nature, to know Christ and salvation by him, to know the truths of the Gospel, and to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts. It is probable that the teachers and ministers of the word were at that time neglected, and this shewed the basest ingratitude: how disgraceful is it to defraud of their temporal support those by whom our souls are fed, to refuse an earthly recompense to those from whom we receive heavenly benefits! But it is, and always has been, the disposition of the world freely to bestow on the ministers of Satan every luxury, and hardly to supply godly pastors with necessary food. Though it does not become us to indulge too much in complaint, or to be too tenacious of our rights, Paul found himself called upon to exhort the Galatians to this part of their duty, and was the more ready to do so because he had no private interest in the matter, but consulted the universal benefit of the Church. Give the diagnosis: he saw that the ministers of the word were neglected because the word itself was despised, for if the word be truly esteemed its ministers will always receive kind and honourable treatment; and it is one of the tricks of Satan to defraud godly ministers of support, that the Church may be deprived of such ministers. Set the limit as well: he does not propose that no limit should be set to their worldly enjoyments, or that they should revel in superfluous abundance. On the warning, name the deceivers and the deceived. They might be deceived by false teachers, who, in order to engross all to themselves, dissuaded the Galatians from communicating to their honourable pastors and to the faithful ministers of the word; or by themselves, who, being of a tenacious and covetous disposition, devised various things to excuse them from performing this duty — that they had families of their own to maintain, that their circumstances were such that they could give little or nothing this way, and that others of better abilities in life ought to bear this charge — and with such things endeavoured to satisfy their consciences in the neglect of their duty; but this was all self-deception. Meet the excuses directly: the design of the observation is to reply to the dishonest excuses which are frequently pleaded, and the consequence of them is that, while such multitudes withhold their aid, the few persons who do their duty are generally unable to contribute the necessary support. Paul utterly rejects these apologies, for a reason which the world little considers, that this transaction is with God: the supply of a man’s bodily wants is not the sole question, but the degree of our regard for Christ and his gospel. The custom of treating faithful ministers with scorn did not originate in the present day, but their wicked taunts will not pass unpunished. Then answer the fear behind the excuses with the seed: our liberality is restrained by the supposition that whatever passes into the hands of another is lost to ourselves, and by the alarm we feel about our own prospects in life; but no operation is more cheerfully performed by husbandmen than throwing the seed into the ground, and they are enabled to wait with patience during nine months of the year by the expectation of reaping a corruptible harvest, while our minds are not properly affected by the hope of a blessed immortality.

Warn against the show of religion. Many excuse themselves from the work of religion, though they may make a show and profess it; they may impose upon others, yet they deceive themselves if they think to impose upon God, who knows their hearts as well as their actions, and as he cannot be deceived, so he will not be mocked. Then state the principle simply: our present time is seed time, and in the other world we shall reap as we sow now. As there are two sorts of sowing, one to the flesh and the other to the Spirit, so will the reckoning be hereafter.

Put the duty as a matter of plain justice. He who receives instruction in Christianity by the public preaching of the word is to contribute to the support of the man who has dedicated himself to the work of the ministry, and who gives up his time and his life to preach the Gospel; let him that is taught impart to him that teacheth all such temporal good things as he stands in need of. It appears that some of the believers in Galatia could receive the Christian ministry without contributing to its support, and this is both ungrateful and base. We do not expect that a common schoolmaster will give up his time to teach our children their alphabet without being paid for it; and can we suppose that it is just for any person to sit under the preaching of the Gospel, in order to grow wise unto salvation by it, and not contribute to the support of his spiritual teacher? It is unjust. On the warning: neither deceive yourselves, nor permit yourselves to be deceived by others — he seems to refer to the Judaizing teachers. God is not mocked: ye cannot deceive him, and he will not permit you to mock him with pretended instead of real services; they attempt to mock him who think to reap otherwise than they sow. And keep the figure agricultural: whatsoever kind of grain a man sows in his field, of that shall he reap, for no other species of grain can proceed from that which is sown — darnel will not produce wheat, nor wheat, darnel.

Begin by admitting you once thought the commandment needless, and say what changed. Here he preacheth to the hearers of the word, commanding them to bestow all good things upon those which have taught and instructed them. I have sometimes marvelled why the Apostles commanded the churches so diligently to nourish their teachers; for in Popery I saw that all men gave abundantly to the building and maintaining of goodly temples, and to the increasing of the revenues and livings of those which were appointed to their idolatrous service, so that the estimation and riches of the bishops and the rest of the clergy did so increase that everywhere they had in possession the best and most fruitful grounds. Therefore I thought that Paul had commanded this in vain, seeing that all manner of good things were not only abundantly given to the clergy, but they also overflowed in wealth and riches; wherefore I thought that men ought rather to be exhorted to withhold their hands from giving than encouraged to give any more, for I saw that by this excessive liberality of men the covetousness of the clergy did increase. But now I know the cause why they had such abundance of good things heretofore, and now the pastors and ministers of the word do want. Beforetime, when nothing else was taught but errors and wicked doctrine, they had such plenty of all things that of Peter’s patrimony — who denied that he had either silver or gold — and of spiritual goods, as they called them, the Pope was become an emperor, and the cardinals and bishops were made kings and princes of the world. But now, since the Gospel hath been preached and published, the professors thereof be as rich as sometime Christ and his Apostles were. Then turn the threatening on the despisers. The Apostle prosecuteth this place of the nourishing and maintaining of ministers so earnestly that to his former reprehension and exhortation he addeth now also a threatening: God is not mocked. And here he toucheth to the quick the perverseness of those who proudly despise our ministry, for they think it to be but a sport and a game, and therefore go about to make their pastors subject unto them like servants and slaves. When the pastors ask their duty, or complain that they suffer penury, they cry out, The priests be covetous, they would have plenty, no man is able to satisfy their insatiable covetousness; if they were true gospellers they should have nothing of their own, but as poor men ought to follow poor Christ and to suffer all adversities. Paul horribly threateneth here such tyrants and such mockers of God, who so carelessly and proudly do scorn the miserable preachers, and yet will seem to be gospellers and not mockers of God, but to worship him very devoutly. Be not deceived, saith he, God is not mocked — that is to say, he doth not suffer himself to be mocked in his ministers; for he saith, He that despiseth you despiseth me, and he said unto Samuel, They have not cast thee away, but me. Therefore, O ye mockers, although God defer his punishment for a season, yet when he seeth time he will find you out, and will punish this contempt of his word and the bitter hatred which ye bear against his ministers. Therefore ye deceive not God, but yourselves.

debates: Whether the teachers of the Galatian churches formed a distinct paid class.
What communicating in all good things requires, and whether any limit is set to it.
Why the ministers of the word were being neglected.
Whether the solemnity of God is not mocked suits an exhortation about money.
outliers: Luther says he had thought the apostolic command needless, and explains what changed his mind.
Calvin traces the neglect of ministers to contempt for the word itself.
Gill fixes on the word catechumen and denies it means a beginner.
Ellicott concedes the warning may seem too solemn for its occasion.

8.pericope_label: For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting. And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not. As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith

schools.summary: Define the sowing and then the reaping. He that soweth to his flesh makes provision for the indulgence of fleshly appetites and passions, using his property to give indulgence to licentiousness, intemperance and vanity. Punishment under the divine government is commonly in the line of offences: the punishment of licentiousness and intemperance in this life is commonly loathsome and offensive disease, and when long indulged the sensualist becomes haggard and bloated and corrupted and sinks into the grave; and if punishment does not follow in this life, it will overtake him in the world to come. Take corruption at three depths: by disease; in the grave, the home to which the sensualist rapidly travels; and in the world of woe, where all shall be corrupt, his virtue and even the semblance of virtue gone, his understanding, will and fancy — his whole soul — debased. On the other side, he that soweth to the Spirit follows the leading and cultivates the affections which the Holy Spirit would produce, and shall reap life everlasting. On weariness, note that the reference is particularly to the support of the ministers of religion, but that the exhortation is made general. Christians sometimes become weary: there is so much opposition to the best plans for doing good, so much to be done, so many calls on their time and their charities, and often so much ingratitude among those whom they endeavour to benefit, that they become disheartened. Exhort such not to give over, but to persevere; in due season means at the day of judgment, when we shall receive the full reward of all our self-denials and charities. It is implied that unless a man perseveres in doing good to the end of life he can hope for no reward: he who becomes disheartened, who is appalled by obstacles, who pines for ease and withdraws from the field of benevolence, shows that he has no true attachment to the cause. He who becomes a true Christian becomes such for eternity; he has enlisted, never to withdraw. On the last verse, give the true rule about doing good: the opportunity to do good imposes the obligation to do it. It is not that we are to do it when it is convenient, or when it will advance the interest of a party, or when it may contribute to our fame; the rule is that we are to do it when we have the opportunity, no matter how often that occurs, no matter how many objects of benevolence are presented — the more the better — no matter how much self-denial it may cost us, no matter how little fame we may get by it. And it is to be done to all men: not to our family only, not to our party, not to our neighbours, not to those of our own colour, not to those who live in the same land with us, but to all mankind; if we can reach and benefit a man who lives on the other side of the globe, whom we have never seen and shall never see in this world or in the world to come, still we are to do him good. Such is Christianity, and in this it differs from the narrow and selfish spirit of clanship which prevails all over the world. Elsewhere put the metaphor plainly: the seed sown is a man’s actions here on earth, and if the object of those actions is merely self-indulgence they are sown, as it were, in a field the owner of which is the flesh, so that the flesh alone benefits by them and for it alone are they garnered up; he must look to the flesh for his reward, and all the reward it can give him is a share in its own corruption. Where the actions are like seed deposited in the field of which the owner and lord is the Spirit, that same Spirit will reward them in the world to come with the gift of everlasting life. Read the next verse as But rather than And, with a stress on well-doing continuing the idea of sowing to the Spirit; and for be weary read rather, let us not be faint-hearted, lose heart. Take therefore as emphatic and first in the sentence, introducing a summary conclusion from the preceding argument. On the household of faith, allow that the translation may stand: the Greek word, meaning originally a member of a household, came to mean simply belonging to, the idea of a household being dropped; but in view of the passage where the saints are called fellow citizens and of the household of God, with its play upon city and house, it ought here to be retained, and the Church is elsewhere represented as a household. Elsewhere again keep to the words: corruption is an old word whose precise meaning turns on the context, here plainly the physical and moral decay or rottenness that follows sins of the flesh, for nature writes in one’s body the penalty of sin, as every doctor knows. Let us not be weary is a volitive present subjunctive, literally, let us not keep on giving in to evil while doing the good — and it is curious how prone we are to give in and to give out in doing the good which somehow becomes prosy or insipid to us. In due season is at its proper season, harvest time; if we faint not is literally not loosened out, relaxed, exhausted as a result of giving in to evil. As we have opportunity means as we have occasion at any time, and let us work that which is good means let us keep on working the good deed. Of the household of faith is said for the obvious reason that they belong to the same family, with the responsibility that follows.

Say first what sowing to the flesh is not. Taking due care of a man’s body, seeking the preservation of its health, providing proper food and raiment for himself and all necessaries for the good and support of his family, is not to be called sowing to his flesh, nor is such a man to be called a carnal sower. The carnal sower is he that pampers his flesh, gratifies and indulges the lusts of it, minds the things of the flesh, lives after it and does the works of it, who spends his substance in a luxurious way upon himself and family; or whose whole bent and study and employment is to increase his worldly riches and to aggrandise himself and his posterity, to the neglect of his own soul, the interest of religion, the poor of the church and the ministers of the Gospel. Then divide the general sentiment into its parts. To sow to the flesh is to look forward to the wants of the present life without any regard to a future life; they who do this will gather fruit corresponding to the seed which they have sown, and will heap up that which shall miserably perish. Some suppose the phrase to mean indulgence in the lusts of the flesh, and corruption to mean destruction, but the former exposition agrees better with the context; and in departing from the old translation and from Erasmus I have not acted rashly, for the Greek words signify literally sowing to his own flesh — and what else does this mean, but to be so entirely devoted to the flesh as to direct all our thoughts to its interests or convenience? By the Spirit understand the spiritual life, to which they are said to sow whose views are directed more to heaven than to earth, and whose life is regulated by the desire of reaching the kingdom of God; from their spiritual employments they will reap in heaven incorruptible fruit. Those employments are denominated spiritual on account of their end, though in some respects they are external and relate to the body, as in the very case now under consideration of supporting pastors. If the Papists shall endeavour, in their usual manner, to build upon these words the righteousness of works, answer that though eternal life is a reward, it does not follow either that we are justified by works or that works are meritorious of salvation: the undeserved kindness of God appears in the very act of honouring the works which his grace has enabled us to perform, by promising to them a reward. On well-doing, note that the word does not simply mean doing our duty, but the performance of acts of kindness, and has a reference to men: we are instructed in assisting our neighbours, in performing good offices, and in exercising generosity. This precept is highly necessary, for we are naturally reluctant to discharge the duties of brotherly love, and many unpleasant occurrences arise by which the ardour of the best disposed persons is apt to be cooled. We meet with many unworthy and many ungrateful persons; the vast number of necessitous cases overwhelms us, and the applications which crowd upon us from every quarter exhaust our patience; our warmth is abated by the coolness of other men; in short, the world presents innumerable hindrances which tend to lead us aside from the right path. Most properly, therefore, does Paul admonish us not to relax through weariness. We shall reap the fruit which God promises, if we persevere to the end. Those who do not persevere resemble indolent husbandmen, who, after ploughing and sowing, leave the work unfinished, and neglect to take the necessary precautions for protecting the seed from being devoured by birds, or scorched by the sun, or destroyed by cold; it is to no purpose that we begin to do good, if we do not press forward to the goal. Let no man, from a wish to gather the fruit in this life, deprive himself of it. On the last verse, pursue the metaphor still: every season is not adapted to tillage and sowing, and active and prudent husbandmen will observe the proper season and will not indolently allow it to pass unimproved; since God has set apart the whole of the present life for ploughing and sowing, let us avail ourselves of the season, lest through our negligence it be taken out of our power. Opportunity may also be rendered ability, as occasion requires and objects offer, while the time of life lasts, which is the time for sowing. Beginning with liberality to ministers of the gospel, Paul now makes a wider application and exhorts us to do good to all, but recommends to our particular regard believers, because they belong to the same family with ourselves: there are duties which we owe to all men arising out of a common nature, but the tie of a more sacred relationship, established by God himself, binds us to believers.

Set the two harvests against each other and refuse the middle way. He that sows to the flesh, who indulges his sensual and animal appetites, shall have corruption as the crop: you cannot expect to lead a bad life and go to heaven at last. According as your present life is, so will be your eternal life; whether your sowing be to the flesh or to the Spirit, so will your eternal reaping be. To sow here means transacting the concerns of a man’s natural life; to reap signifies his enjoyment or punishment in another world. Offer also a further identification: probably by flesh and Spirit the apostle means Judaism and Christianity, for circumcision of the flesh was the principal rite of the former and circumcision in the heart, by the Spirit, the chief rite of the latter; hence the one may have been called flesh and the other Spirit. He who rejects the Gospel and trusts only in the rites and ceremonies of the law for salvation will reap endless disappointment and misery; he who trusts in Christ and receives the gifts and graces of the Holy Spirit shall reap life everlasting. On weariness: well-doing is easier in itself than ill-doing, and the danger of growing weary in it arises only from the opposition to good in our own nature, or from the outward hindrances we may meet with from a gainsaying and persecuting world. As the husbandman, in ploughing, sowing, and variously labouring in his fields, is supported by the hope of a plentiful harvest which he cannot expect before the right and appointed time, so every follower of God may be persuaded that he shall not be permitted to pray, weep, deny himself, and live in conformity to his Maker’s will, without reaping the fruit of it in eternal glory. Guard the point carefully: although no man obtains glory because he has prayed, yet none can expect glory who do not seek it in this way; this is sowing to the Spirit, and the Spirit and the grace are furnished by Christ Jesus, by whom the kingdom of heaven is opened to all believers — but only those who believe, love and obey shall enter into it. Let us persevere in sowing to the Spirit; when the harvest is come we shall reap, if we faint not. On the last verse, take the opportunity broadly: at whatever time or place, and in whatever manner we can. The opportunity in general is our lifetime, but there are also many particular opportunities; and since Satan is quickened in doing hurt by the shortness of the time, by the same consideration let us be quickened in doing good. Let us do good in every possible kind and in every possible degree, unto all men, neighbours or strangers, good or evil, friends or enemies — but especially to them who are of the household of faith, for all believers are but one family, and the members of the Church of Christ form one family of which Jesus Christ is the head. Those have the first claims on our attention, but all others have their claims also.

Take the similitude and apply it to the matter in hand. He that soweth in the Spirit, that is, he that cherisheth the teachers of God’s word, doth a spiritual work and shall reap everlasting life; and he that soweth in the flesh, that is, he that giveth nothing to the ministers of God’s word but only feedeth and careth for himself, which is the counsel of the flesh, shall of the flesh reap corruption, not only in this present life but also in the life to come, for the goods of the wicked shall waste away and they themselves shall at length shamefully perish. Here riseth a question, whether we deserve eternal life by good works, for so Paul seemeth to avouch in this place. Answer that it is very necessary, after the example of Paul, to exhort the faithful to good works, that is to say, to exercise their faith by good works; for if they follow not faith, it is a manifest token that their faith is no true faith. The Apostle would fain stir up his hearers to be liberal and beneficial towards their pastors and preachers — and what a misery is it that the perverseness and ingratitude of men should be so great that the churches should need this admonition. On the next verse, note that the Apostle, intending to close up his Epistle, passeth from the particular to the general, and exhorteth generally to all good works. As if he should say, let us be liberal and bountiful, not only towards the ministers of the word but also towards all other men, and that without weariness; for it is an easy matter for a man to do good once or twice, but to continue, and not to be discouraged through the ingratitude and perverseness of those to whom he hath done good, that is very hard. Therefore he doth not only exhort us to do good, but also not to be weary in doing good; and to persuade us the more easily thereunto he addeth, in due time we shall reap without weariness — as if he said, wait and look for the perpetual harvest that is to come, and then shall no ingratitude or perverse dealing of men be able to pluck you away from well doing, for in the harvest time ye shall receive most plentiful increase and fruit of your seed. Thus with most sweet words he exhorteth the faithful to the doing of good works. On the last verse, which is the knitting up of his exhortation for the liberal maintaining of the ministers of the word and the giving of alms to all such as have need: as if he had said, let us do good while it is day, for when night cometh we can no longer work. Indeed men work many things when the light of truth is taken away, but all in vain, for they walk in darkness and wot not whither they go, and therefore all their life, works, sufferings and death are in vain. And by these words he toucheth the Galatians: except ye continue in the sound doctrine which ye have received of me, your working of much good and your suffering of many troubles profit you nothing — as he said before, have ye suffered so many things in vain? And by a new kind of speech he termeth those the household of faith which are joined with us in the fellowship of faith, among whom the ministers of the word are the chiefest, and then all the rest of the faithful.

debates: What sowing to the flesh includes, and whether ordinary provision for a family falls under it.
Whether flesh and Spirit here stand for Judaism and Christianity.
Whether the promised reaping makes eternal life a reward earned by works.
What the household of faith means, and whether the domestic sense survives in the Greek.
outliers: Clarke identifies flesh and Spirit with Judaism and Christianity by way of the two circumcisions.
Gill lists what sowing to the flesh is not, beginning with the care of one’s own body and family.
Calvin defends his departure from the old translation and from Erasmus on the phrase sowing to his own flesh.
Luther applies the whole similitude narrowly to the maintenance of ministers before generalising it.
Barnes makes the opportunity itself the whole obligation, with no qualification allowed.

11.pericope_label: Ye see how large a letter I have written unto you with mine own hand. As many as desire to make a fair shew in the flesh, they constrain you to be circumcised; only lest they should suffer persecution for the cross of Christ. For neither they themselves who are circumcised keep the law; but desire to have you circumcised, that they may glory in your flesh

schools.summary: Settle the enigmatic phrase, or admit it cannot be settled. The word rendered how large means properly how great. Some suppose it refers to the size of the letters in which Paul wrote — the length and crudeness of the characters he used — supposing that he was not well versed in writing Greek, and used large letters, somewhat rudely made, like the Hebrew; so Doddridge and Whitby interpret it, and so Theodoret, Jerome, Theophylact and others. He might not, says Doddridge, have been well versed in the Greek characters, or the inaccuracy of his writing may have been owing to the infirmity or weakness of his nerves; Jerome says he was a Hebrew, unacquainted with the mode of writing Greek letters, and that because necessity demanded a letter in his own hand, contrary to his usual custom, he was obliged to form his characters in this crude manner. On that reading the handwriting was both a pledge to the Galatians that the epistle was genuine, since it bore the marks of his own hand, and a proof of special affection, that he was willing to undergo this labour on their account. Elsewhere be more exact. Read See rather than Ye see; and read, in what large letters, that is, characters. Two points are clear: the latter part of the phrase means in or with letters, that is, characters of handwriting, and not a letter or an epistle; and the former half means how large, strictly in respect of size. The apostle, for some reason, points out that the characters in which he is writing are larger than usual, and what his reason is, is hard to say. Some have thought the reference is to the shapelessness of the letters, whether from the apostle’s being unaccustomed to the manual work of writing or from physical weakness after his hardships; but the idea of shapelessness is not necessarily included in that of size. It seems on the whole most probable that the size of the characters expresses the emphasis and authority with which the apostle is writing: he adds to the Epistle, which so far had been written by an amanuensis, a few bold incisive strokes in his own hand, trenchantly exposing the motives of the Judaising faction and re-asserting his own position. Elsewhere again, take the pen from the amanuensis with him. He writes the rest of the Epistle himself instead of the mere farewell greeting, and by with how large letters he certainly does not mean how large a letter. It has been suggested that he employed large letters because of defective eyesight, or because he could only write ill-formed letters, like the print letters of children, or because he wished to call particular attention to this closing paragraph by placarding it in big letters; this last is the most likely. Note the contrast often seen in the papyri between the neat hand of the scribe and the big sprawling hand of the signature. I have written is an epistolary aorist. On the Judaisers, say what they are after: to be distinguished for their conformity to external rites and customs, and to be known for their zeal in that cause, showing it by making converts and inducing others to conform. They insist on circumcision as indispensable to salvation, and not from any true love to the cause of religion, but that they may avoid persecution from the Jews; if they renounced the doctrine that circumcision is indispensable they would be exposed to Jewish rage. This verse shows the true cause of the zeal which the Judaizing teachers evinced: it was the fear of persecution, the want of independence and boldness in maintaining that men are to be saved only by the merits of the Lord Jesus; by attempting to blend the doctrines of Judaism and Christianity, and maintaining that the observance of Jewish rites was necessary and yet that Jesus was the Messiah, they endeavoured to keep in with both parties. Add the historical mechanism: what aroused the antagonism of the Jews against the Christians was evidently not so much the confession of the Messiahship of Jesus as the declared abolition of the Law of Moses, so that by suppressing this side of Christian teaching the Judaisers could easily obtain toleration for their other tenets; if on the other hand they emphasised it, the full weight of persecution would fall upon them, its ostensible ground being the doctrine of a crucified Messiah. Accordingly they persuaded as many of the Galatians as they could to accept circumcision, and made the most of this propagandist zeal to their Jewish neighbours. On the last verse, press the inconsistency: if they were circumcised they brought themselves under obligation to keep the whole law, but no man perfectly observes the whole law of God, the Jewish nation as such were very far from doing it, and it is probable that these persons did not even pretend to keep the whole law of Moses — probably they did not offer sacrifice, or join in the numerous observances of the Jewish nation, except some of the more prominent, such as circumcision. This is inconsistent in the highest degree, and they thus show their insincerity and hypocrisy. That they may glory in your flesh is equivalent to, in your circumcision: making use of your circumcision to promote their own importance and to save themselves from persecution. Their insincerity is shown by the fact that they are not really careful to observe the Law; what they do is only to serve as a blind, that they may be able to point to your mutilated flesh as the visible sign of their success in gaining proselytes. The expression they themselves who are circumcised includes in the Greek not only those who were circumcised themselves but also those who were for circumcising others; note too that some manuscripts read they who have been circumcised, but the present participle, those who are having themselves circumcised, is probably correct as the harder reading.

Take the phrase of the length of the letter, and say why. Whether it be read as imperative, see ye, observe, take notice, or as indicative, ye see, ye do see, is of no great consequence. Some understand how large a letter of the largeness of the characters he wrote in, others of the deformity of them, he not writing a good hand, being a Hebrew and not used to writing Greek, others of the grand and sublime matter which it contained; but none of these seems to be the apostle’s meaning. He intends the length of the epistle, the prolixity of his writing, which he mentions as an instance and expression of his love to them, his care of them and his concern for them, inasmuch as he took so much pains to write so long a letter in order to set things right in their view and recover them from error — though he had sent as long or longer letters to other churches. The meaning of the Greek verb is so far doubtful that it may be taken either in the imperative or the indicative mood, but the force of the passage is little if at all affected: to convince the Galatians more fully of his anxiety about them, and at the same time to ensure their careful perusal, he mentions that this long Epistle had been written with his own hand, and the greater the toil to which he had submitted on their account, the stronger were their inducements to read it, not in a superficial manner, but with the closest attention. On the Judaisers, expose their aims and ends. They were very desirous to carry a good face of things outwardly, to appear outwardly righteous before men and to be accounted so by them, and therefore did all to be seen of them and to gain applause from them; the Syriac renders it, such as desired to glory in the flesh, that is, in their carnal descent and privileges, in being Hebrews, the seed of Abraham, of the stock of Israel, and in the circumcision of their flesh, or in their external gifts, natural parts, acquired abilities and eloquence. The Vulgate reads, they were willing to please in the flesh, that is, to please carnal men, Israel after the flesh, in carnal and fleshly things; they sought not to please God or Christ, but men, and so were the servants of neither. Charge them with ambition. Such men pay no regard to edification, but are guided by an ambitious desire to hunt after popular applause: when those men lay circumcision upon you as a necessary burden, do you wish to know what sort of persons they are? You are mistaken if you imagine that they are at all influenced by godly zeal; to gain or preserve the favour of men is the object they have in view in offering this bribe. It was because they were Jews that they adopted this method of retaining the good-will, or at least allaying the resentment, of their own nation; and it is the usual practice of ambitious men meanly to fawn on those from whose favour they hope to derive advantage, and to insinuate themselves into their good graces, that, when better men have been displaced, they may enjoy the undivided power. On the last verse, correct the translation and then press the charge.
