The old version and Erasmus make it all circumcised persons; but Paul appears to refer to teachers only, and for that reason the words should be rendered so as not to include all circumcised persons, and thus to avoid ambiguity. The meaning is: it is not from a strong attachment to the law that they bind you with the yoke of ceremonies, for even with their own circumcision they do not keep the law; it is no doubt under the pretext of the law that they require you to be circumcised, but though they have themselves been circumcised they do not perform what they enjoin upon others. It is doubtful whether the whole law or the ceremonies are meant; some understand him as saying that the law is an intolerable burden and therefore they do not satisfy its demands, but he rather insinuates against them a charge of insincerity, because, except when it suited their own designs, they found themselves at liberty to despise the law. Even now this disease rages everywhere with virulence: you will find many who are prompted more by ambition than by conscience to defend the tyranny of the papal system — courtly apostles, attracted by the smell of a kitchen, who pronounce with an air of authority that the decrees of the holy Church of Rome must be observed with reverence, and whose own practice all the while is to pay no more regard to any decisions of the Roman see than to the braying of an ass, but to take care to avoid personal risk. Paul had the same kind of controversy with those impostors as we now have with hypocritical professors. Note finally that they that are circumcised means the pleaders for and preachers of circumcision, whether they themselves were actually circumcised or not.

Explain why the epistle does not end where it seems to. Having at large established the doctrine of the gospel, and endeavoured to persuade these Christians to a behaviour agreeable to it, the apostle seems as if he intended here to have put an end to the epistle, especially when he had acquainted them that, as a particular mark of his respect, he had written this large letter with his own hand, and had not made use of another as his amanuensis, only subscribing his name as he was wont to do in his other epistles. But such is his affection to them, such his concern to recover them from the bad impressions made upon them by their false teachers, that he cannot break off till he has once again given them the true character of those teachers, and an account of his own contrary temper and behaviour, that by comparing these together they might the more easily see how little reason they had to depart from the doctrine he had taught them and to comply with theirs. Then give that character. They were men who desired to make a fair show in the flesh: very zealous for the externals of religion, forward to observe, and to oblige others to observe, the rites of the ceremonial law, though at the same time they had little or no regard to real piety — for, as the apostle says of them in the following verse, neither do they themselves keep the law. Proud, vain and carnal hearts desire nothing more than to make a fair show in the flesh, and are content with just so much religion as will help to keep up a fair show.

Argue for the length, and dismiss the notion that Paul could not write Greek. There is a strange diversity of opinions concerning the apostle’s meaning: some think he refers to the length of the epistle, others to the largeness of the letters in which it is written, others to the inadequacy of the apostle’s writing. It appears plain that most of his epistles were written by an amanuensis and simply subscribed by himself, but the whole of the Epistle to the Galatians was written by his own hand; he had not yet written a larger to any church. To say that the apostle was unskilled in Greek, and especially in the Greek characters, is in my opinion absurd. He was born in Tarsus, a city which, according to Strabo, rivalled both Athens and Alexandria in philosophy and in arts and sciences, and therefore he could not be ignorant of a tongue which must have been the very means of conveying all this instruction; and as to writing it, there was in his time nothing difficult, because the uncial character was that which alone was in use, and this character is as easily made as the capitals in the Roman alphabet, which have been taken from it. I conclude therefore that what the apostle says must be understood of the length of the epistle, in all probability the largest he had ever written with his own hand. On the Judaisers, give the local reason for their conduct. The Jewish religion was general in the region of Galatia, and it was respectable, as it appears that the principal inhabitants were either Jews or proselytes; and as it was then professed and practised among the Jews, this religion had nothing very grievous to the old man — an unrenewed nature might go through all its observances with little pain or cross-bearing. On the other hand, Christianity could not be very popular: it was too strict. A Jew made a fair show there, according to his carnal system, and it was a temptation to a weak Christian to swerve into Judaism, that he might be exempted from persecution and be creditable among his countrymen. They constrain you both by their example and their importunity, to be circumcised, not so much from a principle of conscience as lest they should suffer persecution from the unbelieving Jews for the cross of Christ — that is, for maintaining that faith in a crucified Saviour is alone sufficient for justification. On the last verse: they receive circumcision and profess Judaism, not from a desire to be conformed to the will of God, but because Judaism was popular, and the more converts the false teachers could make, the more occasion of glorying they had. So far are they from a real zeal for the law that neither do they themselves keep the whole of it; but they wished to get those Christian converts who had before been proselytes of the gate to receive circumcision, that they might glory in their flesh. Behold my converts! Thus they gloried, or boasted, not that the people were converted to God, but that they were circumcised, making a merit of this with the other Jews.

Close the Epistle with an exhortation and a sharp invective. Behold, saith he, what a letter I have written unto you with mine own hand. This he saith to move them, and to show his motherly affection towards them: as if he should say, I never wrote so long an epistle with mine own hand to any other church as I have done unto you. As for his other Epistles, as he spake, others wrote them, and afterwards he subscribed his salutation and name with his own hand, as is to be seen at the end of them; and in these words, as I suppose, he hath respect to the length of the Epistle, though some take it otherwise. Then accuse the false apostles very sharply, to the end he may fear and turn away the Galatians from their doctrine, notwithstanding the great authority which they seemed to have. The teachers which ye have, saith he, are such as, first, regard not the glory of Christ and the salvation of your souls, but seek only their own glory; secondly, they fly the cross; thirdly, they understand not those things which they teach. Being accused of three such execrable enormities, they were worthy to be avoided of all men. Paul doeth the false apostles no wrong when he so vehemently inveigheth against them, but justly condemneth them by his apostolic authority; in like manner, when we call the Pope Antichrist, and his bishops and his shavelings a cursed generation, we slander them not, but by God’s authority judge them to be accursed, according to that which he said in the first chapter, if we, or an angel from heaven, preach otherwise than we have preached unto you, accursed be he; for they hate, persecute and overthrow the doctrine of Christ. Because they are afraid of the cross, they preach circumcision and the righteousness of the flesh, lest they should provoke the Jews to hate and persecute them. On the last verse, meet the objection that this makes Paul a heretic. He saith that not only the false apostles but all the nation of the Jews which were circumcised keep not the law, but rather that they which were circumcised, in fulfilling the law, fulfil it not; and this seems against Moses, who saith that to be circumcised is to keep the law, and not to be circumcised is to make the covenant void, and the Jews were circumcised for no other cause but to keep the law, which commanded that every male child should be circumcised the eighth day. Answer that these things serve to the condemning of the false apostles, that the Galatians may be scared from hearing them: behold, I set before your eyes what manner of teachers you have — first they are vainglorious men, which seek nothing but their own profit and care for nothing but their own belly; secondly, they fly the cross; and finally, they teach no truth or certainty, but all their sayings and doings are counterfeit and full of hypocrisy. Wherefore, although they keep the law outwardly, yet in keeping it they keep it not; for without the Holy Ghost the law cannot be kept, and the Holy Ghost cannot be received without Christ, and where the Holy Ghost dwelleth not, there dwelleth an unclean spirit, despising God and seeking his own gain and glory. Therefore all that he doth, as touching the law, is mere hypocrisy and double sin.

debates: Whether the phrase means a long letter or characters of unusual size.
Whether Paul was unskilled in writing Greek characters.
What moved the Judaising teachers to press circumcision.
Whether they themselves who are circumcised means the teachers only or all circumcised Jews.
outliers: Clarke calls the notion that Paul could not write Greek absurd, and cites Strabo on Tarsus.
Ellicott makes the large characters a mark of emphasis and authority rather than of infirmity.
Robertson prefers Ramsay’s reading, that Paul placarded the closing paragraph in big letters.
Calvin restricts the circumcised of verse 13 to the teachers, and says so against the old version and Erasmus.
Luther answers the charge that Paul is here contradicting Moses on circumcision.

14.pericope_label: But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision, but a new creature. And as many as walk according to this rule, peace be on them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God

schools.summary: Set the apostle against the party he has been describing. His object is to place himself in contrast with the Judaizing teachers and to show his determined purpose to glory in nothing else but the cross of Christ; and they knew well that he had as much occasion for glorying in the things pertaining to the flesh as any of them. He had been circumcised; he had had all the advantages of accurate training in the knowledge of the Jewish law; he had entered on life with uncommon advantages, and had evinced a zeal not surpassed by any of them, his life being blameless so far as conformity to the religion in which he had been trained was concerned. By placing his own conduct in strong contrast with theirs, and showing that he had no ground of confidence in himself, he designed to bring the Galatians back to simple dependence on the cross. Others glory in their conformity to the laws of Moses, others in their zeal, or their talents, or their learning, or their orthodoxy; others in their wealth, or their accomplishments; others in their family alliances and their birth: but the supreme boast and glorying of a Christian is in the cross of Christ. On the new creature, say that the fact that a man is created anew, or born again, constitutes the real difference between him and other men: it is not by conformity to certain rites and customs that a man is accepted, nor by elevated rank, nor by wealth, or beauty, or blood, nor by the colour of the complexion, but the grand inquiry is whether he is born again and is in fact a new creature in Christ Jesus. On the last verse, walk means live, as the word is used in the Scriptures; the word for rule is properly a canon; and the Israel of God is the true church of God, all who are his true worshippers. Elsewhere note the emphasis and the paradox. There is a stress upon the pronoun I, which in the Greek stands first, in emphatic contrast to the party who were the subjects of the last verse: they make their boast in a mere external, but for me, far be it from me to make my boast in anything but the cross of Christ, that is, in the death and passion which Christ underwent for me. The apostle is aware that in this he is putting forward a startling paradox: the cross of Christ was to the Jews a stumbling-block, and they attached to it only ideas of ignominy and shame, and yet it is precisely this of which the apostle is most proud — proud of it as the ground of his salvation, and therefore as the cardinal object of all his hopes and aims. On by whom, it seems better on the whole to adopt the marginal rendering, whereby: the antecedent is thus not Christ but more especially the cross of Christ, for it is the intense contemplation of a crucified Saviour through which the Christian dies to the world. By the world is meant here the world of sense, the sphere of outward and sensible things, at once with its manifold temptations to sin and with its inadequate methods of escaping from them — mere external rites, such as circumcision. Note that the words in Christ Jesus are omitted by the Vatican manuscript and by the best editors, and would seem to have come in from the parallel passage earlier in the epistle. It is interesting to note the different ways in which this sentence is completed elsewhere: circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but faith which worketh by love; a new creature; keeping the commandments of God. The first is an analytical statement of the process which takes place in the Christian, the second is the state resulting from that process, and the last is the visible sign and expression of the presence of that state. The Greek for a new creature may mean either the act of new creation or the person newly created, and the latter is perhaps to be preferred. The word for rule is the same that afterwards received a special application in the phrase, Canon of Scripture: it meant originally a carpenter’s rule, or the line that a carpenter works by, hence a rule or standard, and from that the list of books coming up to a certain standard, not — as might be thought — which themselves supplied a standard. The apostle confines his benediction to those who hold the fundamental truths of Christianity, here more especially the doctrine of justification by faith and the spiritual view of Christianity connected with it, as opposed to the merely external and mechanical system of the Judaisers. And the benediction is addressed, not to two distinct sets of persons, but to the same set described in different ways, so that and is equivalent to namely: yea, upon the Israel of God, by which is meant the spiritual Israel, not converts from Judaism alone, but all who prove their real affinity to Abraham by a faith like Abraham’s. Elsewhere again keep to the grammar: far be it from me is a second aorist middle optative in a negative wish about the future with the dative, may it not happen to me; hath been crucified unto me is the perfect passive, stands crucified, with the ethical dative again. This is one of the great sayings of Paul concerning his relation to Christ and the world in contrast with the Judaizers, and his old world of Jewish descent and environment is dead to him. World has no article but is definite.

Say what he refuses to glory in, and then what he does. He expresses his aversion to glorying in anything these men did: not in his outward carnal privileges as a Jew, nor in his moral, civil and legal righteousness, nor in his gifts and attainments, nor in his labours and success as of himself, nor in the flesh of others, or in any outward corporeal subjection to any ordinance, legal or evangelical; his glorying and rejoicing were rather in the spirituality, the faith, hope, love, patience, order and steadfastness of the saints than in anything in the flesh, either his own or others. Set the designs of the false apostles against his own sincerity: to avoid being compelled to bear a cross, they deny the cross of Christ, purchase with your flesh the applause of men, and end by triumphing over you; but my triumph and my glory are in the cross of the Son of God. If the Galatians had not been utterly destitute of common sense, ought they not to have held in abhorrence the men whom they beheld making sport of their dangerous condition? To glory in the cross is to glory in Christ crucified, but something more is implied: in that death — so full of disgrace and ignominy, which God himself has pronounced to be accursed, and which men are wont to view with abhorrence and shame — he will glory, because he obtains in it perfect happiness; for where man’s highest good exists, there is his glory. But why does he not seek it elsewhere? Though salvation is held out to us in the cross of Christ, what of his resurrection? Answer that in the cross redemption in all its parts is found, and the resurrection of Christ does not lead us away from the cross. And let it be carefully observed that every other kind of glorying is rejected by him as nothing short of a capital offence. On by whom, note that as the Greek word for cross is masculine the relative pronoun may be rendered either by whom or by which, according as we refer it to Christ or to the cross. The reason he is crucified to the world, and the world to him, is that in Christ, to whom he is spiritually united, nothing but a new creature is of any avail: everything else must be dismissed, must perish — I refer to those things which hinder the renewing of the Spirit. If any man wishes to be considered as belonging to the kingdom of Christ, let him be created anew by the Spirit of God; let him not live any longer to himself or to the world, but let him be raised up to newness of life. The truth of the gospel swallows up, and brings to nought, all the shadows of the law. On the rule, say what it may be: not the canon of the Scriptures in general, which is the perfect rule and only standard of faith and practice, but either the doctrine of justification by the righteousness of Christ, the subject of this epistle, which to depart from is going out of the way of truth, and which is a good standard by which to distinguish between truth and error, since whatever is contrary to that article of faith cannot be true; or else the rule delivered in the preceding verse, that circumcision and uncircumcision are of no avail in salvation, but a new creature — and to walk according to that rule is to renounce all trust in and dependence upon any outward things, to believe alone in Christ for righteousness and life, and to walk in newness of life. Then take the benediction as approbation as well as prayer: those who teach this doctrine are worthy of all esteem and regard, and those who reject it do not deserve to be heard. The word denotes the regular and habitual course which all godly ministers of the gospel ought to pursue: architects employ a model in the erection of buildings, to assist them in preserving the proper form and just proportions, and such a rule does the apostle prescribe to the ministers of the word, who are to build the church according to the pattern shewn to them. Faithful and upright teachers, and all who conform to this rule, must derive singular encouragement from this passage, in which God, by the mouth of Paul, pronounces on them a blessing; we have no cause to dread the thunders of the Pope if God promises to us from heaven peace and mercy. Note that the future tense of the verb is intended to express perseverance.

State what makes the difference between men, and then what is promised. A new creation to the image of Christ, as showing faith in him, is the greatest distinction between one man and another, and a blessing is declared on all who walk according to this rule. The blessings are peace and mercy: peace with God and our conscience, and all the comforts of this life so far as they are needful; and mercy, an interest in the free love and favour of God in Christ, the spring and fountain of all other blessings. The written word of God is the rule we are to go by, both in its doctrines and its precepts.

Refuse every other ground of exultation. Whatever others may do, or whatever they may exult or glory in, God forbid that I should exult, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ — in the grand doctrine that justification and salvation are only through Christ crucified, he having made an atonement for the sin of the world by his passion and death; and I glory also in the disgrace and persecution which I experience through my attachment to this crucified Christ. Should boast of anything I have, am, or do, or rely on anything for my acceptance with God, but what Christ hath done and suffered for me. By whom the world is crucified unto me: Jewish rites and Gentile vanities are equally insipid to me, for I know them to be empty and worthless; if Jews and Gentiles despise me, I despise that in which they trust, and through Jesus all are crucified to me — their objects of dependence are as vile and execrable to me as I am to them, in whose sight these things are of great account. All the things and persons in the world are to me as nothing, and I am dead to all worldly pursuits, cares, desires and enjoyments. On the new creature, insist on the noun. Under the dispensation of the Gospel, of which Christ is head and supreme, neither circumcision — nothing that the Jew can boast of, nothing that the Gentile can call excellent — availeth anything, or can in the least contribute to the salvation of the soul; but a new creation. Not a new creature merely, for this might be restrained to any new power or faculty, but a total renewal of the whole man, of all the powers and passions of the soul; and as creation could not be effected but by the power of the Almighty, so this change cannot be effected but by the same energy. No circumcision can do this: only the power that made the man at first can new make him; and whereby all things in us become new. On the rule, say what canon is meant: what is laid down in the preceding verses, that redemption is through the sacrifice of Christ, that circumcision and uncircumcision are equally unavailable, and that none can be saved without being created anew. This is the grand canon or rule in Christianity, and those who act from this conviction will have the peace and mercy of God, for it is in this way that mercy is communicated and peace obtained. The Israel of God means the true Christians, so called to distinguish them from Israel according to the flesh — the Church, which consists of all those, and those only, of every nation and kindred, who walk by this rule.

Take the two clauses as a mutual sentence and say what each means. The world is crucified to me: that is, I judge the world to be damned. And I am crucified to the world: that is, the world judgeth me to be damned. Thus we crucify and condemn one another. I abhor all the doctrine, righteousness and works of the world as the poison of the devil; the world again detesteth my doctrine and deeds, and judgeth me to be seditious, a pernicious, a pestilent fellow, and an heretic. So at this day the world is crucified to us, and we unto the world: we curse and condemn all men’s traditions concerning mass, orders, vows, will-worshippings and works as the dirt of the devil, and they again persecute and kill us as destroyers of religion and troublers of the public peace. Correct the monastic use of the words: the monks dreamed that the world was crucified to them when they entered into their monasteries, but by this means Christ is crucified and not the world — yea, the world is delivered from crucifying, and is the more quickened by that opinion of holiness and trust which they had in their own righteousness. Most foolishly and wickedly therefore was this sentence of the Apostle wrested to the entering into monasteries. He speaketh here of an high matter and of great importance, that is to say, that every faithful man judgeth that to be the wisdom, righteousness and power of God which the world condemneth as the greatest folly, wickedness and weakness. On the next verse, call it a wonderful kind of speech. It may seem that he should rather have said, either circumcision or uncircumcision availeth somewhat, seeing these are two contrary things; but he denieth that either the one or the other doth any thing avail. As if he should have said, ye must mount up higher, for circumcision and uncircumcision are things of no such importance that they are able to obtain righteousness before God. True it is that they are contrary the one to the other, but this is nothing as touching Christian righteousness, which is not earthly but heavenly, and therefore consisteth not in corporal things: whether thou be circumcised or uncircumcised, it is all one thing. The Jews were greatly offended when they heard that circumcision availed nothing, for they fought even unto blood for the defence of the law and circumcision; and the Papists at this day do vehemently contend for the maintenance of their traditions touching the eating of flesh, single life, holy days and such other, and they excommunicate and curse us who teach that in Christ Jesus these things do nothing avail. But Paul saith that we must have another thing, much more excellent and precious, whereby we may obtain righteousness before God. On the last verse, add it as a conclusion: this is the only and true rule wherein we ought to walk, namely the new creature, which is neither circumcision nor uncircumcision, but the new man created unto the image of God in righteousness and true holiness, which inwardly is righteous in the Spirit and outwardly is holy and clean in the flesh. The monks have a righteousness and holiness, but it is hypocritical and wicked, because they hope not to be justified by only faith in Christ, but by the keeping of their rule; and although outwardly they counterfeit a holiness, and refrain their eyes, hands and tongue from evil, yet they have an unclean heart.

debates: Whether by whom refers to Christ or to the cross.
What is meant by the world that is crucified.
Whether a new creature means the act of new creation or the person newly created.
What rule is meant, and who the Israel of God are.
outliers: Luther reads the two crucifixions as a mutual sentence of damnation passed between the believer and the world.
Luther denies that the verse has anything to do with entering a monastery.
Calvin asks why Paul glories in the cross rather than the resurrection, and answers from the cross itself.
Ellicott reports that in Christ Jesus is absent from the Vatican manuscript and the best editors.
Clarke presses new creation against new creature, as a total renewal rather than a new faculty.

17.pericope_label: From henceforth let no man trouble me: for I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus

schools.summary: Say what trouble is meant. From henceforth means for the remaining time, that is, during the remainder of my life; and let no man trouble me implies that he had had trouble of some kind, and earnestly desires that he may have no more. What particular trouble is not certainly known, and commentators have not agreed; but the connexion requires us to understand it of the molestation he had suffered in regard to his call to the apostolic office, and his authority to explain and defend the religion of the Redeemer, which has been a principal subject of this epistle. His authority had been called in question; he had felt it necessary to go into a vindication of it; his instructions had been departed from on the ground that he was not one of the original apostles and that he differed from others; and hence all the anxiety he had felt about their departure from the doctrines he had taught them. He closes the whole subject with tender and affecting language, whose sense has been well expressed thus: I have shown my apostolic authority, and proved that I am commissioned by the Lord Jesus; I have stated and vindicated the great doctrine of justification by faith, and shown that the Mosaic law is not necessarily binding; on these points may I have no more trouble, for I have enough of other kinds for my nature to bear. I bear in my body the impressive proofs that I am an apostle, and the sufferings that require all my fortitude to sustain them; these marks, received in the service of the Lord Jesus, and so strongly resembling those which he himself received, prove that I am truly engaged in his cause and commissioned by him. Elsewhere say the apostle has done: he will not dally with these vexatious attacks upon himself and his authority any more, but dismisses them with an appeal which ought to be final. He points to the scars of wounds received in his Master’s service — the branding-irons of Christ, he says, have imprinted these upon me; they show that I, like the slaves of a heathen temple, am devoted and consecrated to his service; they are my credentials, and I shall produce no others; my assailants must leave me in peace. On the word itself: the stigmata are marks inflicted with branding-irons, such as show that a slave is attached to a particular temple or to the service of some particular deity. Branding was applied in some other cases, but especially to temple slaves, and those with which the Galatians were most familiar would be engaged in the worship of Cybele. There does not seem to be evidence to connect this passage directly with the incident of the stigmata in the life of St Francis of Assisi, but it would seem very probable that the use of the word, which was left untranslated in the Latin versions, suggested, whether by a nearer or a more distant association, the idea which took so strong a hold upon his mind that in a moment of extreme spiritual tension the actual marks of the Passion seemed to imprint themselves upon his body. Note that the true text reads simply, of Jesus. Elsewhere again keep to the grammar and the custom. From henceforth is usually the accusative of general reference, as for the rest; the genitive case, as here, means in respect of the remaining time. The word for marks is an old one from a verb meaning to prick, to stick, to sting. Slaves had the names or stamp of their owners on their bodies; it was sometimes done for soldiers also; and there were devotees who stamped upon their bodies the names of the gods whom they worshipped — today in a round-up cattle are given the owner’s mark. Paul gloried in being the slave of Jesus Christ, and this is probably the image in his mind, since he bore in his body brandmarks of suffering for Christ received in many places, probably actual scars from the scourgings, thirty-nine lashes at a time. If for no other reason, listen to him by reason of these scars for Christ, and let no one keep on furnishing trouble to him.

Take the words as a requirement, not a request. Having so clearly stated and explained the doctrine of justification, and so largely proved that it is not by works but by faith, and that circumcision and the other rituals of the ceremonial law were not necessary to it, he desires — nay, in an authoritative way he requires — that they give him no further trouble on that head; signifying that he expected they would be satisfied with what he had written, and abide by the truth and obey it as they had formerly done, and that he should hear no more objections from them or complaints of them. Nor need they further inquire his sense of these things: by this they would fully know his faith and practice, as indeed they might also by his suffering persecutions on account of his faith and his preaching the Gospel of Christ. Then take the voice of authority. He now speaks for restraining his adversaries, and employs language which his high rank fully authorised: let them cease to throw hindrances in the course of my preaching. He was prepared, for the sake of the church, to encounter difficulties, but does not choose to be interrupted by contradiction; let no man make opposition to obstruct the progress of my work. The phrase means, as to everything besides: this one thing is enough for me, other matters are of no importance and give me no concern, let no man question me about them. He thus places himself above all men, and allows to none the power of attacking his ministry. Literally the phrase signifies as to the rest, which Erasmus, in my opinion, has improperly applied to time. On the marks, note that a Greek expositor observes that Paul does not say I have, but I bear, as some trophy or royal symbol, and I deck myself with them; this accounts for his bold, authoritative language. And what were those marks? Imprisonment, chains, scourging, blows, stoning, and every kind of injurious treatment which he had incurred in bearing testimony to the gospel. Earthly warfare has its honours, in conferring which a general holds out to public view the bravery of a soldier; so Christ our leader has his own marks, of which he makes abundant use for conferring on some of his followers a high distinction. These marks, however, differ from the others in one important respect, that they partake of the nature of the cross, and in the sight of the world are disgraceful; and this is suggested by the word itself, for it literally denotes the brand with which barbarian slaves, or fugitives, or malefactors were usually branded.

Make the appeal pastoral before it is personal. Put an end to your contentions among yourselves; return to the pure doctrine of the Gospel; abandon those who are leading you astray; separate from the Church those who corrupt and disturb it; and let me be grieved no longer with your defections from the truth — let none trouble me by quarrels and disputes, for afflictions should not be added to the afflicted. Then set out the two senses of the marks. The stigmata may be understood as implying the scars of the wounds which he had received in the work of the ministry; and that he had such scars we may well conceive, knowing that he had been scourged, stoned, and maltreated in a variety of ways. Or the apostle may allude to the stigmata or marks with which servants and slaves were often impressed, in order to ascertain whose property they were — a Burman servant often has indelible marks on his thighs and elsewhere, which ascertain to whose service he belongs. On that reading he says: do not trouble me, I bear the marks of my Lord and Master Jesus, I am his and will remain so; you glory in your mark of circumcision, I glory in the marks which I bear in my body for the testimony of the Lord; I am an open, professed Christian, and have given full proof of my attachment to the cause of Christianity. But the first sense appears the best: I have suffered already sufficiently, I am suffering still, do not add any more to my afflictions. The marks are the scars, marks and brands of my sufferings for him.

Conclude the Epistle with a certain indignation. As if he said, I have faithfully taught the Gospel as I have received it by the revelation of Jesus Christ; whoso will not follow it, let him follow what he will, so that hereafter he trouble me no more. At a word, this is my censure, that the Christ which I have preached is the only High Priest and Saviour of the world; therefore either let the world walk according to this rule, of which I have spoken here and throughout all the Epistle, or else let it perish for ever. This is the true meaning of the place: the marks that be in my body do show well enough whose servant I am. If I sought to please men, requiring circumcision and the keeping of the law as necessary to salvation, and rejoicing in your flesh as the false apostles do, I needed not to bear these marks in my body. But because I am the servant of Jesus Christ, and walk after a true rule — that is, I openly teach and confess that no man can obtain the favour of God, righteousness and salvation but by Christ alone — therefore it behoveth me to bear the badges of Christ my Lord; which be not marks of mine own procuring, but are laid upon me against my will by the world and the devil, for none other cause but for that I preach Jesus to be Christ. The stripes and sufferings therefore which he did bear in his body he calleth marks, as also the anguish and terror of spirit he calleth the fiery darts of the devil; and of these sufferings he maketh mention everywhere in his Epistles.

debates: What trouble the apostle is asking to be spared.
Whether from henceforth is a note of time or means as to the rest.
Whether the marks are scars of persecution or the brands of a slave.
Whether the marks are a disgrace or a decoration.
outliers: Calvin denies that the opening phrase is temporal at all, against Erasmus and against the others here.
Ellicott traces the word to temple slaves, and to the Galatians’ own familiarity with the worship of Cybele.
Ellicott suggests the untranslated Latin word suggested the stigmata of Francis of Assisi.
Clarke illustrates branding from the indelible marks on the thighs of a Burman servant.

18.pericope_label: Brethren, the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen

schools.summary: Keep the closing note brief and refer the reader onward. Brethren, the grace, and so forth: compare the parallel closes of the other epistles. The farewell salutation is much briefer than the one at the end of Second Corinthians, but identical with that at the end of Philemon; and he calls them brethren in spite of the sharp things spoken to them. On with your spirit, note that the grace of God works especially on the spirit, or highest part, of man. On the subscription, note that as it stands in our Bibles it appears for the first time in manuscripts dating from about the beginning of the ninth century, though before this the Epistle had been described as written from Rome by several of the fathers; the choice really lies between Ephesus and Macedonia, or Corinth, and the probability seems somewhat in favour of the latter. Where nothing further is offered on the verse itself, an appended conjecture on the thorn in the flesh may be set down. St Paul’s infirmity was one well known in hot climates, a chronic ophthalmia; hence he was what is called blear-eyed, and was often perhaps obliged to wear a shade. It made his personal appearance mean; it was a visible infirmity in his flesh; it hindered his usefulness, and therefore he besought the Lord anxiously that it might depart from him. It made it, for the most part, painful and difficult to write, hence he generally employed an amanuensis, and regarded it as a great matter when he used his own pen. The calling of it a messenger of Satan is perfectly consistent with its being a bodily disease, since Satan is in many places represented as the immediate author of corporeal defects and maladies; and it is quite probable that the supernatural light which blinded him at his conversion might have left a weakness and disease in the organs immediately affected, unless the miracle which restored Paul to sight removed also the natural secondary defect of the temporary injury those organs had received. On this supposition the temptation in his flesh which the Galatians did not despise nor reject, and their readiness, if it had been possible, to pluck out their own eyes and give them to him, are both accounted for.

Say why he calls them brethren, and then what he asks for them. He so calls them to testify his affection for them, notwithstanding their infirmity and instability, and the roughness with which he had treated them; and to show his great humility and condescension in owning the relation, and putting them on a level with himself, which the pride of the false teachers would not suffer them to do. On the grace, it is of little moment whether we understand by it that free love and favour which he always bears in his heart to all that believe in his name, or all that kindness — all those heavenly and spiritual blessings — in the communication of which he manifests this love and free favour. But do not pass over the last words. His prayer is not only that God may bestow upon them his grace in large measure, but that they may have a proper feeling of it in their hearts; then only is it truly enjoyed by us, when it comes to our spirit. We ought therefore to entreat that God would prepare in our souls a habitation for his grace. Amen.

Expand the blessing and then deal with the subscription. The grace is the favour, benevolence and continual influence of the Lord Jesus: be it with your spirit — may it live in your heart, enlighten and change your souls, and be conspicuous in your life. Amen: so let it be, and the prayer which I offer up for you on earth, may it be registered in heaven. Then treat the subscription critically. Written from Rome, or the major part of it, is wanting in the best and most ancient manuscripts; one authority reads, written from Ephesus; some add, by the hands of Paul, others, by Titus; the Syriac has, the end of the Epistle to the Galatians, which was written from the city of Rome; the Ethiopic has only, to the Galatians; the Coptic, written from Rome; the Vulgate, nothing; the Arabic, written from the city of Rome by Titus and Luke. Little respect is to be paid to these subscriptions: the epistle was written by Paul himself, not by Titus, Luke or Tychicus, and there is no evidence that it was written from Rome, but rather from Corinth or Ephesus. Close with a retrospect. The great similarity between the Epistle to the Romans and that to the Galatians has been remarked by many, and indeed it is so obvious that the same mode of interpretation may safely be pursued in the elucidation of both, since not only the great subject but the phraseology, in many respects, is the same. The design of the apostle is to show that God has called the Gentiles to equal privileges with the Jews, pulling down the partition wall that had separated them, calling all to believe in Christ Jesus, and forming out of the believers of both peoples one holy and pure body.

Make the last words a farewell and let the exposition end with them. This is his last farewell: he endeth the Epistle with the same words wherewith he began. As if he said, I have taught you Christ purely, I have entreated you, I have chidden you, and I have let pass nothing which I thought profitable for you; I can say no more, but that I heartily pray that our Lord Jesus Christ would bless and increase my labour, and govern you with his holy Spirit for ever. Then make your own farewell to those who have heard the exposition: the Lord Jesus Christ, our Justifier and Saviour, who gave unto me the grace and power to expound this Epistle, and to you likewise to hear it, preserve and establish both you and me — which I most heartily desire — that we, daily growing more and more in the knowledge of his grace and in faith unfeigned, may be found unblamable and without fault in the day of our redemption; to whom, with the Father and the Holy Ghost, be glory world without end. Amen.

debates: Why the apostle calls them brethren after so sharp a letter.
What is added by the words with your spirit.
Where the epistle was written from, and what the subscription is worth.
What the thorn in the flesh was, and whether it explains the large letters of verse 11.
outliers: Clarke rejects the subscriptions outright and canvasses six versions against one another.
Ellicott dates the received subscription to manuscripts of about the ninth century.
Barnes appends a conjecture that the apostle’s infirmity was a chronic ophthalmia, which would account for the large letters.
Calvin makes the whole force of the blessing turn on the words with your spirit.
